questions.title: Designing the SFT, Reward Model, and PPO Pipeline Shape
questions.prompt: You are standing up a small-scale RLHF pipeline for the first time on a team. Describe the three stages (SFT, reward model training, PPO) and how data and models flow between them, including what could go wrong if a stage is skipped or under-invested in.
questions.modelAnswer:
The standard pipeline flows in a fixed order because each stage depends on the output of the one before it. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) first takes a pretrained base model and fine-tunes it on demonstration data (prompt-response pairs showing the desired style and behavior), producing a model that can follow instructions reasonably well; this SFT model becomes both the starting point for the policy that PPO will further train and the reference policy that PPO's KL penalty measures against. Reward model training happens in parallel or just after: human annotators compare pairs of responses (often generated by the SFT model itself) and label which is preferred, and a reward model is trained on those comparisons (typically via a Bradley-Terry-style pairwise loss) to predict a scalar preference score for any given response. PPO then uses the SFT model as its starting policy and the reward model as its reward signal, optimizing the policy to generate responses the reward model scores highly, while the KL penalty against the SFT reference policy keeps the policy from drifting into degenerate, reward-hacking behavior.

Skipping or under-investing in SFT means PPO starts from a base model that doesn't reliably follow instructions, so PPO's exploration spends enormous effort doing the SFT model's job (learning to be coherent and on-task at all) before it can even begin optimizing against preferences, often producing unstable, incoherent early training. Under-investing in reward model data quality or quantity is more subtle but arguably worse: a poorly trained reward model is an imperfect proxy that PPO will optimize against as hard as it can, and small reward model errors get amplified by the optimization process into real behavioral problems (reward hacking) that are expensive to discover and fix after the fact. Skipping PPO (SFT plus reward model alone, with no RL step) leaves the model unable to improve beyond whatever the demonstration data showed, missing the gains that come specifically from optimizing against a learned preference signal rather than imitating fixed examples.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd walk through why the order is fixed, not arbitrary. SFT comes first because you need a model that can already follow instructions and respond coherently before you try to optimize it against a preference signal -- it's fine-tuned on demonstration data, and it becomes both the starting policy for PPO and the reference policy PPO's KL penalty measures drift against.

Reward model training happens alongside or right after: you get human annotators to compare pairs of responses and say which is better, and you train a reward model on those comparisons -- usually with a pairwise preference loss -- so it can score any response's quality. Then PPO starts from the SFT model and optimizes it to generate responses the reward model scores highly, with the KL penalty against the SFT model keeping it from drifting into weird, reward-hacking territory.

If I skipped or rushed SFT, PPO would be starting from a model that doesn't reliably follow instructions yet, so a huge amount of PPO's early training would just be relearning basic coherence instead of actually optimizing against preferences -- that's a recipe for an unstable, messy run. If I under-invested in reward model data quality, that's actually the scarier failure mode, because PPO will optimize against whatever the reward model says as hard as it can, and small systematic errors in the reward model get amplified into real behavioral problems that are expensive to catch after the fact rather than before. And if I skipped PPO entirely, the model would be capped at whatever the demonstration data showed -- you lose the actual benefit of optimizing against a learned preference signal instead of just imitating fixed examples.
questions.example: Concretely: SFT model trained on ~10-50k demonstration pairs; reward model trained on ~50-100k+ pairwise human comparisons (often generated by sampling the SFT model); PPO then runs the SFT model as policy+reference against that reward model, typically for far fewer total gradient steps than either SFT or reward model training required.
commonMistakes: Treating the three stages as interchangeable or reorderable rather than sequentially dependent
Under-investing in SFT and expecting PPO to compensate for a weak base policy
Under-investing in reward model data quality, underestimating how much errors get amplified by PPO optimization
Skipping PPO and assuming SFT alone captures the full benefit of RLHF
Not using the SFT model consistently as both the PPO starting policy and the KL reference
keyPoints: SFT produces both the PPO starting policy and the KL reference policy
Reward model training uses pairwise human preference comparisons, often on SFT model outputs
PPO optimizes the SFT policy against the reward model with a KL penalty to the SFT reference
Weak SFT investment destabilizes PPO by forcing it to relearn basic coherence
Weak reward model investment is amplified into real behavioral problems by PPO's optimization pressure

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes the three-stage pipeline and data/model flow
Explains the consequence of under-investing in SFT
Explains the consequence of under-investing in the reward model
Explains the consequence of skipping PPO

questions.title: Reproducibility Under Deadline Pressure
questions.prompt: You are two days from a deadline to report results, and you realize you forgot to fix the random seed and log the exact config for your best run so far. Rerunning from scratch with proper logging might not finish in time. What do you do?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer treats this as a disclosure problem first and a scheduling problem second: whatever gets reported needs to be honest about exactly what was and was not properly logged, since reporting an unreproducible result as if it were fully reproducible is a bigger problem than the result itself being slightly uncertain. The candidate should describe immediately starting a properly seeded, fully logged rerun in parallel with preparing the report, so there is at least a chance of having confirmed, reproducible numbers before the deadline, rather than discovering the gap and doing nothing about it until it's too late to even attempt a fix.

The candidate should also describe what can be salvaged from the original run even without a fixed seed: checking whatever partial logging did happen (checkpoints, any config files or git commits saved, environment details) to reconstruct as much of the exact setup as possible, and running a few replicate seeds of the same config going forward to establish the result's variance, which gives the team a confidence interval around the original number even if the exact original run can never be perfectly reproduced.

If the rerun doesn't finish in time, the answer should describe being explicit in the report about the limitation: presenting the original number with a clear note that it is not yet confirmed reproducible, alongside whatever replicate runs did finish, rather than quietly presenting the original number as if the logging gap didn't exist. Cutting corners on honesty about reproducibility to hit a deadline undermines the team's ability to trust and build on the result later, which costs far more time than the deadline saves.
questions.professionalAnswer:
First thing I'd do is kick off a properly seeded, fully logged rerun immediately, in parallel with everything else -- even if it might not finish before the deadline, starting it right away gives it the best chance of landing in time, and doing nothing about it until it's too late would be the worse mistake.

While that's running, I'd see what I can actually salvage from the original run -- any checkpoints, partial logs, config files, or even just the git commit I was on at the time -- to reconstruct as much of the original setup as I can. I'd also queue up a couple of replicate seeds of the same config so I at least have a sense of the result's variance, even if I can't perfectly reproduce the exact original run.

If the full rerun doesn't finish by the deadline, I'd be straightforward about it in the report rather than quietly presenting the number as if nothing were wrong. Something like, 'this result is from a run where I didn't fix the seed or fully log the config -- here's what I've reconstructed, and here are N replicate runs with the same config showing it's stable within this range.' I'd rather own that gap clearly than have someone discover later that a reported number can't actually be reproduced, because that costs a lot more trust than just being upfront about it now.
questions.example: Report framing that preserves trust: 'Original result: 74.2% (seed not fixed, partial logging). 3 replicate runs with the same config and fixed seeds: 73.1%, 74.8%, 73.9% -- result appears stable within ~1.5 points.'
commonMistakes: Silently reporting the unreproducible result as if it were fully confirmed
Doing nothing about the gap because a full rerun seems unlikely to finish in time
Not attempting to salvage partial logging/checkpoint information from the original run
Skipping replicate seeds, leaving no variance estimate even as a partial substitute
Prioritizing hitting the deadline over being honest about a real reproducibility gap
keyPoints: Starts a properly seeded, fully logged rerun immediately in parallel with reporting
Salvages whatever partial logging/checkpoint data exists to reconstruct the original setup
Runs replicate seeds to establish a variance estimate even without perfect reproduction
Is explicit and honest in the report about exactly what is and isn't confirmed
Treats honesty about reproducibility as more important than hitting the deadline cleanly

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Takes immediate action to start a properly logged rerun
Proposes salvaging partial information and running replicates
Commits to honest disclosure of the limitation in the report
Demonstrates appropriate prioritization of rigor over deadline optics

questions.title: What Actually Transfers When Fine-Tuning a Pretrained Vision Model
questions.prompt: Explain what happens, layer by layer, when you take a pretrained vision model and fine-tune it on a new, smaller image classification task. Why does freezing early layers often work well, and when does it not?
questions.modelAnswer:
Pretrained vision models learn a rough hierarchy of features across their layers: early layers tend to learn generic, low-level patterns like edges, textures, and simple color/contrast gradients that are useful across almost any natural image task, while later layers learn increasingly task-specific, higher-level combinations of those features that are more specialized to the original training objective (for example, specific object-part detectors tuned to the original dataset's classes). This is why a common transfer learning strategy is to freeze the early layers entirely (keeping those generic low-level features unchanged) and only fine-tune the later layers plus a new final classification head on the new, smaller dataset -- the early layers' generic features are likely to be useful regardless of the new task, and freezing them means far fewer parameters need to be updated, which both reduces overfitting risk on a small new dataset and cuts training cost.

This works well when the new task's images are visually similar in low-level statistics to the original pretraining data (natural photos, similar lighting/color distributions) and the new task mainly differs in what high-level categories matter. It works less well when the new domain is visually quite different at a low level from the original pretraining distribution -- medical imaging, satellite imagery, or line-art/sketches, for example, where even the 'generic' early-layer features learned from natural photos may not transfer well, because the low-level statistics of the new domain genuinely differ from what the early layers were tuned to extract. In those cases, unfreezing more layers (or all of them, with a low learning rate) and fine-tuning further down the hierarchy, or even considering training more from scratch, tends to perform better than naively freezing layers calibrated to a visually different domain.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd describe it as a rough hierarchy: early layers in a pretrained vision model tend to pick up generic stuff like edges and textures that shows up in basically any natural image, while later layers get more specialized, building up toward whatever specific object categories the original task cared about. That's the whole reason freezing early layers and only fine-tuning the later layers plus a new classification head works as a default strategy -- the generic low-level features are probably useful no matter what the new task is, and freezing them means way fewer parameters to update, which helps a lot when the new dataset is small and overfitting is a real risk.

Where that breaks down is when the new domain looks genuinely different at a low level from what the model was originally trained on -- medical scans, satellite imagery, sketches, that kind of thing. In those cases even the 'generic' early features might not actually be that generic for this new domain, because they were tuned to natural-photo statistics that don't really hold here. When I see that mismatch, I'd unfreeze more of the network, probably with a lower learning rate across more layers, or in extreme cases just consider that transfer learning from this particular pretrained model isn't buying me much and train more from scratch.
questions.example: Fine-tuning a natural-image pretrained model on chest X-rays is a classic case where naive early-layer freezing underperforms, because X-ray low-level statistics (contrast, texture, lack of color) differ enough from natural photos that even the 'generic' early features aren't a great match.
commonMistakes: Assuming early-layer freezing always works regardless of how different the new domain is
Not recognizing the rough low-level/high-level feature hierarchy across layers
Fine-tuning the entire network at a high learning rate on a small dataset, risking overfitting
Treating transfer learning as domain-agnostic rather than dependent on visual similarity to the pretraining distribution
Not considering unfreezing more layers when results on a visually different domain are poor
keyPoints: Early layers learn generic low-level features; later layers learn task-specific high-level features
Freezing early layers reduces parameters to update, helping with small datasets and training cost
This strategy works best when the new task is visually similar at a low level to the pretraining data
It works poorly when the new domain's low-level statistics differ substantially from the original data
Unfreezing more layers or training further is the right response in a visually dissimilar domain

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes the layer-wise feature hierarchy
Explains why freezing early layers is a reasonable default
Correctly identifies when this strategy fails
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: What the Pretrain, SFT, and Align Stages Each Actually Change
questions.prompt: A newcomer to the team asks why an LLM needs three separate training stages (pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and alignment/RL) instead of just one big training run. Explain what each stage is actually optimizing for and why they can't be collapsed into one.
questions.modelAnswer:
Pretraining optimizes a next-token prediction objective over a massive, mostly unstructured text corpus, and what it actually produces is a model with broad language competence and world knowledge, but no particular tendency to be helpful, follow instructions, or behave like an assistant -- it is just as willing to continue a prompt in an unhelpful, rambling, or unsafe direction as a helpful one, because 'predict plausible next text' doesn't distinguish those. Supervised fine-tuning takes that base model and trains it further on a much smaller, curated dataset of prompt-response demonstrations, which shifts the model's default behavior toward the specific style and structure of being a helpful assistant -- but it is still just imitating fixed demonstrations, so it can only be as good as the demonstrations themselves and has no mechanism to learn from outcomes it wasn't explicitly shown.

Alignment (typically RLHF/RLAIF) optimizes against a learned reward signal reflecting human (or AI) preferences over many possible responses, which lets the model improve beyond what any fixed set of demonstrations could show it, because it is optimizing against comparative judgments across a wide space of its own generated outputs rather than imitating a fixed answer. These three stages can't be collapsed into one run because each depends on the output of the previous one: there is no comparative preference signal to optimize against before you have a model capable of generating coherent, on-topic candidate responses, and there is no reasonable set of demonstrations to imitate before the model has the base language competence pretraining provides. Each stage is also optimizing a genuinely different objective (next-token likelihood on raw text, versus imitation of curated demonstrations, versus a learned preference signal), and conflating them into one loss function would require weighting fundamentally incompatible signals against each other from the very start of training, when the earliest signal (pretraining) hasn't even produced a model capable of being meaningfully evaluated by the later ones yet.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd explain it as each stage doing a genuinely different job, in an order where each one depends on the last. Pretraining is just next-token prediction over a huge, mostly unstructured text corpus -- what you get out of that is broad language ability and world knowledge, but the model has no particular lean toward being a helpful assistant; it'll continue a prompt in whatever direction looks statistically plausible, helpful or not.

SFT takes that base model and trains it on a much smaller set of curated demonstrations of what a helpful response actually looks like, which shifts its default behavior toward that style. But it's still just imitation -- it can only be as good as those demonstrations, and it has no way to learn from outcomes it wasn't explicitly shown examples of.

Alignment, usually RLHF, is where the model actually optimizes against a learned preference signal across many of its own candidate responses, which lets it improve past what any fixed demonstration set could teach it directly.

The reason you can't collapse these into one run is that each one needs the output of the previous stage to even make sense. You can't train a reward model or run RL against a model that can't yet generate coherent, on-topic responses -- that's what pretraining and SFT exist to produce first. And you can't curate a good demonstration set to imitate before the model has basic language competence. They're solving different problems in sequence, not one problem split into three parts.
questions.example: A raw pretrained base model given 'How do I reset my password?' might continue with something plausible-sounding but unhelpful or off-topic; the same prompt after SFT reliably gets a direct, on-task answer; after alignment, the answer additionally tends to better match what humans actually preferred across many compared response pairs, not just what the demonstration set happened to show.
commonMistakes: Describing pretraining as already producing 'assistant-like' behavior
Treating SFT and alignment as redundant or interchangeable
Not explaining the dependency chain (each stage needs the previous stage's output to function)
Assuming more pretraining data could substitute for SFT or alignment
Missing that alignment can improve beyond what any fixed demonstration set could teach
keyPoints: Pretraining optimizes next-token prediction, producing broad competence but no assistant-like default behavior
SFT imitates curated demonstrations, bounded by the quality of those demonstrations
Alignment optimizes against a learned preference signal, enabling improvement beyond fixed demonstrations
Each stage depends on the previous stage's output to function at all
The three stages optimize genuinely different objectives that can't be meaningfully combined from scratch

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what pretraining produces and its limits
Correctly explains what SFT adds and its limits
Correctly explains what alignment adds beyond SFT
Explains the dependency chain preventing collapse into one stage

questions.title: Implementing Tabular Q-Learning
questions.prompt: Write the core update rule for tabular Q-learning and explain why it is an off-policy algorithm despite the agent following its own policy to collect data.
questions.code:
Q = {}  # dict mapping (state, action) -> value, defaults to 0

def update(state, action, reward, next_state, done):
    # TODO: implement the Q-learning update
    pass
questions.modelAnswer:
The Q-learning update rule is Q(s,a) <- Q(s,a) + alpha * (reward + gamma * max_a' Q(s', a') - Q(s,a)) (with the max term zeroed out if the episode terminated), where alpha is the learning rate, gamma is the discount factor, and the term in parentheses is the temporal-difference error -- the difference between the current estimate and a better estimate built from the actual observed reward plus the best possible value achievable from the next state. The key detail is the max over a' in the target: regardless of which action the agent actually took next (which is determined by whatever exploration policy, e.g. epsilon-greedy, it is following), the update always bootstraps toward the value of the best action available from the next state.

This is exactly why Q-learning is off-policy: the policy generating the data (the behavior policy, often epsilon-greedy for exploration) can differ from the policy whose value is actually being learned (the target policy, which is implicitly the greedy policy that always takes the max-value action). An on-policy method like SARSA would instead use the Q-value of whatever action the agent actually takes next under its current behavior policy, making the learned value a direct reflection of that exploratory policy's behavior rather than the purely greedy policy. Q-learning's off-policy property is what lets it learn the optimal greedy policy's values even while exploring with a different, non-greedy behavior policy, and more generally lets it learn from any data regardless of what policy generated it (including old replayed experience), which is part of why it combines well with experience replay.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The update is Q(s,a) += alpha * (reward + gamma * max over a' of Q(s', a') - Q(s,a)), using zero for the bootstrap term if the episode ended. The part that matters most is the max over a' -- no matter what action the agent actually ends up taking next under whatever exploration policy it's using, the target always bootstraps toward the best possible value from the next state, not whatever action actually gets taken.

That's exactly the reason Q-learning is off-policy. The policy collecting the data -- usually epsilon-greedy, so it explores sometimes -- is different from the policy whose values are actually being learned, which is implicitly the fully greedy policy because of that max in the target. Something like SARSA, by contrast, uses the value of whatever action actually gets taken next under the current exploratory policy, so it's learning the value of the policy it's actually following, which makes it on-policy.

The practical payoff of being off-policy is that Q-learning can learn from data generated by a different policy than the one it's evaluating -- including old experience sitting in a replay buffer -- which is exactly why it pairs so naturally with experience replay in methods like DQN.
commonMistakes: Using the value of the actually-taken next action instead of the max over all next actions
Forgetting to zero out the bootstrap term when the episode has terminated
Confusing the behavior policy (used to act) with the target policy (whose value is being learned)
Claiming Q-learning is on-policy because the agent generates its own data
Not connecting the off-policy property to why experience replay works with Q-learning
keyPoints: The update bootstraps toward the max Q-value over next actions, not the actually-taken action
This max is what makes Q-learning off-policy: it learns the greedy policy's values regardless of the behavior policy
SARSA is the on-policy counterpart, using the actually-taken next action's value instead
Terminal states should zero out the bootstrap term
The off-policy property enables learning from replayed or differently-generated data

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly writes the Q-learning update rule
Correctly explains the max-over-actions target
Correctly explains why this makes Q-learning off-policy
Contrasts correctly with an on-policy method (e.g. SARSA)

questions.title: Diagnosing Catastrophic Forgetting After Fine-Tuning
questions.prompt: After fine-tuning a model on a narrow customer-support dataset, you notice it has gotten noticeably worse at general reasoning tasks it previously handled well. How do you confirm this is catastrophic forgetting and what are your options to fix it?
questions.modelAnswer:
To confirm this is catastrophic forgetting rather than a coincidental regression or an evaluation artifact, the first step is running the model on a broad, standard evaluation suite covering the general capabilities that seemed to degrade, comparing scores directly against the pre-fine-tuning checkpoint on the identical suite -- a clear, consistent drop specifically on general-capability benchmarks, isolated from improvement on the new narrow task, is the signature of forgetting rather than a measurement fluke. It's also worth checking whether the drop is uniform across general tasks or concentrated in capabilities that are especially dissimilar from the fine-tuning data's style and content, since forgetting tends to hit harder on capabilities that share little structural overlap with what was heavily reinforced during fine-tuning.

Once confirmed, the available fixes trade off training cost against how much forgetting is tolerable. Switching from full fine-tuning to a parameter-efficient method like LoRA reduces forgetting risk substantially, since the base weights stay frozen and only a small adapter changes, directly limiting how much the model's general behavior can drift. Mixing a sample of general-capability data back into the fine-tuning set (rehearsal) is another standard fix, explicitly reminding the model during fine-tuning that it still needs to retain broader competence, not just the narrow task. Reducing the learning rate and/or the number of fine-tuning epochs on the narrow data also helps, since aggressive fine-tuning on a small, narrow dataset is exactly what drives the sharpest forgetting; in extreme cases, training a separate lightweight adapter per task and switching between them (rather than one model fine-tuned sequentially on multiple tasks) avoids the forgetting problem entirely by keeping each task's specialization isolated.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I wouldn't just take the anecdotal 'it seems worse now' at face value -- I'd run the model against a broad standard eval suite covering the general capabilities people noticed degrading, and compare those scores directly against the pre-fine-tuning checkpoint on the exact same suite. A clear, consistent drop on general-capability benchmarks that's isolated from the gains on the new narrow task is the real signature of catastrophic forgetting, not just noise or a one-off bad example someone noticed.

I'd also check whether the drop is spread evenly across general tasks or concentrated specifically in capabilities that look structurally different from the customer-support data -- forgetting tends to hit hardest on stuff furthest from what the fine-tuning data was reinforcing.

Once I've confirmed it, my options trade off cost against how much forgetting I can tolerate. Switching to LoRA instead of full fine-tuning is usually my first move, since freezing the base weights directly limits how much general behavior can drift. I'd also mix some general-capability data back into the fine-tuning set as rehearsal, specifically to remind the model it still needs to hold onto that broader competence. And I'd just try fine-tuning less aggressively -- lower learning rate, fewer epochs -- since the sharpest forgetting usually comes from training hard on a small, narrow dataset. If none of that's enough and I genuinely need both behaviors fully intact, I'd consider keeping a separate adapter per task rather than one model that's sequentially specialized away from its general ability.
questions.example: A real pattern: full fine-tuning on 5,000 narrow support examples for 10 epochs drops a general reasoning benchmark by 8 points; switching to LoRA with rank 16 for the same task recovers most of that gap while still hitting the support-task target, at the cost of a slightly longer tuning cycle to find the right rank.
commonMistakes: Confirming forgetting from anecdote alone instead of a direct before/after benchmark comparison
Not isolating whether the drop is concentrated in dissimilar capabilities versus spread evenly
Reaching only for 'train less' without considering LoRA or rehearsal as structural fixes
Assuming any fine-tuning method is equally prone to forgetting
Not considering per-task adapters when both full general and full narrow performance are required simultaneously
keyPoints: Confirm forgetting via a direct before/after comparison on a broad evaluation suite, not anecdote
Forgetting tends to concentrate in capabilities dissimilar to the fine-tuning data
LoRA/PEFT reduces forgetting risk by limiting how much of the model can drift
Rehearsal (mixing general data into fine-tuning) directly counters forgetting
Lower learning rate/fewer epochs reduces forgetting severity; per-task adapters avoid it structurally

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes a rigorous before/after benchmark confirmation method
Proposes LoRA/PEFT as a forgetting-reduction option
Proposes rehearsal/data mixing as a fix
Proposes training intensity reduction or per-task adapters as additional options

questions.title: Choosing Between Full Fine-Tuning and Parameter-Efficient Tuning for a Team
questions.prompt: A team with a single 80GB GPU needs to adapt a 13-billion-parameter model to a new domain and is deciding between full fine-tuning and a parameter-efficient approach. Walk through the architectural decision, including what resource constraints actually rule out.
questions.modelAnswer:
The first question is whether full fine-tuning is even feasible on the available hardware, since that often settles the decision before preference comes into play. Full fine-tuning needs memory for the model weights, gradients for every parameter, and optimizer state (for Adam, roughly two extra values per parameter), plus activation memory for backpropagation; for 13 billion parameters, that typically adds up to well over 150-200GB in fp32 (less with mixed precision and optimizer tricks, but still commonly beyond a single 80GB GPU without techniques like gradient checkpointing, CPU offloading, or sharding across multiple GPUs that this team does not have). That means full fine-tuning on a single 80GB GPU is likely infeasible outright, not just suboptimal, unless combined with aggressive memory-saving techniques that add their own complexity and slow training.

A parameter-efficient approach like LoRA or QLoRA sidesteps this directly: gradients and optimizer state are only needed for the small adapter matrices, not the full 13 billion frozen parameters, which can fit comfortably within a single 80GB GPU (QLoRA additionally quantizes the frozen base weights to 4-bit, shrinking the memory footprint of just holding the model in memory even further). Given the hardware constraint, the architectural decision is less a tradeoff between two viable options and more a recognition that PEFT is the option that actually fits the available resources, with full fine-tuning only becoming viable if the team's hardware budget changes (additional GPUs, model/optimizer sharding) or if the task genuinely requires deeper behavioral change than LoRA can reliably deliver, which should be tested empirically before assuming it.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd start by checking whether full fine-tuning is even possible on this hardware before treating it as a genuine choice. For a 13-billion-parameter model, full fine-tuning needs memory for the weights, gradients for every single parameter, and optimizer state on top of that -- for Adam that's roughly two extra values per parameter -- plus activation memory for backprop. That typically adds up to well over what a single 80GB GPU can hold without serious memory-saving tricks like gradient checkpointing or CPU offloading, which this team doesn't have set up. So in practice, full fine-tuning here isn't really 'the more thorough but slower option,' it's close to infeasible outright on this hardware as-is.

LoRA or QLoRA sidesteps that problem directly, because you only need gradients and optimizer state for the small adapter matrices, not the full 13 billion parameters. QLoRA goes further and quantizes the frozen base model to 4-bit, which shrinks even just holding the model in memory. Given the actual hardware constraint, I wouldn't frame this as weighing two equally viable approaches -- PEFT is the approach that fits what this team actually has. I'd only reconsider full fine-tuning if the hardware budget changes, or if we ran LoRA first and found the task genuinely needs deeper change than it can deliver -- and I'd want to see that empirically before assuming it.

questions.title: Giving Code Review Feedback on Research Code That Cuts a Corner
questions.prompt: You're reviewing a teammate's pull request for a new experiment. The code works and produces results, but it hardcodes a data path, has no seed control, and lacks a config file -- all things that will make the experiment hard to rerun or compare against later. How do you give this feedback?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer frames the feedback around the concrete future cost of each issue rather than as abstract best-practice rule-following, since 'this isn't reproducible' lands better when paired with a specific scenario of what breaks later -- for example, that a hardcoded data path will silently point to the wrong data when someone else tries to rerun the experiment on a different machine, or that missing seed control means nobody, including the original author, can tell later whether a result that looked promising was signal or noise. The candidate should describe being specific and actionable in the review comments rather than vague ('needs more rigor'), ideally suggesting the exact fix (move the path to a config, add an argparse seed flag, extract hyperparameters into a YAML file) so the author can act quickly rather than guessing what 'more rigor' means.

The candidate should also calibrate the severity of the ask to the actual stakes of the experiment: a quick, disposable sanity check that will never be rerun doesn't need the full reproducibility bar, but an experiment whose result will inform a real decision or get reported to the team does, and the reviewer should say which bucket this falls into and why, rather than applying a blanket standard to every PR regardless of its purpose. The answer should avoid making the feedback feel like a referendum on the author's competence -- framing it as 'this will save you time later, not just the reviewer' keeps the tone collaborative rather than gatekeeping.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd make the feedback concrete rather than just flagging 'this isn't reproducible' and leaving it there. For the hardcoded path, I'd say something like, 'this will silently point to the wrong data if anyone else, including future-you on a different machine, tries to rerun this -- can we move it into a config?' For the missing seed, I'd point out that without it, nobody can tell later whether this result was a real effect or just noise from whatever random initialization happened to run, which matters a lot if this result ends up informing a decision.

I'd try to make each comment actionable, not just a complaint -- suggesting the specific fix, like an argparse seed flag or pulling hyperparameters into a YAML file, so they can act on it quickly instead of guessing what I actually want.

I'd also calibrate how hard I push based on what this experiment actually is. If it's a quick throwaway sanity check nobody's going to rerun, I might just leave a light comment and approve anyway. If this result is going to get reported to the team or inform a real decision, I'd be more insistent, and I'd say explicitly why -- 'given this is going into the weekly report, I think we need the config and seed before merging' -- so it doesn't feel like an arbitrary bar, it's tied to the actual stakes of this specific PR.
questions.example: Specific, actionable comment: 'Hardcoded path here will break for anyone else running this -- move to configs/experiment.yaml and read via argparse? Also no seed set -- can we add --seed and log it in the run's output dir name so we can tell runs apart later?'
commonMistakes: Giving vague feedback like 'needs more rigor' without specific, actionable suggestions
Applying the same reproducibility bar to every PR regardless of the experiment's actual stakes
Framing the feedback as a judgment on the author's competence rather than a practical future cost
Not explaining the concrete downstream consequence of each specific issue
Blocking a low-stakes, disposable experiment on the same standard as a decision-informing one
keyPoints: Frames feedback around concrete future costs, not abstract rule-following
Gives specific, actionable suggestions rather than vague requests for 'more rigor'
Calibrates how strictly to enforce reproducibility based on the experiment's actual stakes
Keeps the tone collaborative, framed as saving the author time, not gatekeeping
Explains why the bar is set where it is for this specific PR

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Gives specific, actionable feedback rather than vague comments
Explains concrete downstream consequences of each issue
Calibrates severity to the experiment's actual stakes
Maintains a collaborative, non-judgmental tone

questions.title: Why BPE Merges Are Greedy, Not Globally Optimal
questions.prompt: Explain why byte-pair encoding tokenizer training produces merges one at a time based on local frequency, rather than solving for the single best vocabulary of a given size directly, and what practical consequence this greedy approach has.
questions.modelAnswer:
Finding the single best vocabulary of a fixed size -- the one that would compress a given corpus the most, or optimize some other direct objective -- is combinatorially intractable at the scale of real training corpora, since the space of possible token sets to choose from grows enormous even for modest vocabulary sizes. BPE instead uses a simple, computationally cheap greedy heuristic: repeatedly find whichever adjacent pair of tokens is currently most frequent across the corpus (as tokenized so far, using the current partial vocabulary) and merge it into a new single token, then recompute frequencies and repeat. Each individual merge decision is locally optimal (it merges whatever is most frequent right now) but the overall sequence of merges is not guaranteed to be the globally best possible vocabulary of that size, since an early merge can lock in a token that later turns out to be a slightly worse choice than some alternative that would have required a different, mutually exclusive sequence of merges.

The practical consequence is that BPE's resulting vocabulary is a reasonable, efficient approximation rather than a provably optimal one, and it's also entirely path-dependent on the training corpus's statistics -- the exact same target vocabulary size trained on two different corpora produces two genuinely different vocabularies and merge rules, reflecting whatever local frequency patterns existed in each corpus as the greedy process unfolded. This is generally an acceptable tradeoff because the greedy heuristic is extremely cheap to compute at scale and tends to produce vocabularies that work well in practice, but it does mean token boundaries can sometimes look mildly arbitrary or inconsistent (for example, a common word might be split differently than intuition would expect) as an artifact of the specific merge order that happened to occur, not a deliberate design choice.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd explain it as a tractability tradeoff. Finding the single provably best vocabulary of a given size for a corpus is a combinatorially huge search -- not something you can realistically solve directly at the scale of real training data. BPE sidesteps that by using a cheap greedy rule instead: find whatever adjacent pair is most frequent right now, merge it, recompute, repeat. Each step is locally the best choice available at that moment, but the overall sequence of merges isn't guaranteed to be the best possible vocabulary of that size, because an early merge can lock in a token that blocks a different, possibly better sequence of merges that would've required not making that earlier choice.

The practical consequence is that BPE's vocabulary is a good, efficient approximation, not a provably optimal one, and it's entirely shaped by whatever corpus you trained on -- the same target vocab size on two different corpora gives you genuinely different merge rules and token boundaries. That's also why you sometimes see a token boundary that looks a little odd or arbitrary -- it's usually just an artifact of merge order, not some deliberate linguistic decision. In practice this tradeoff is worth it because the greedy approach is cheap enough to actually run at scale and the resulting vocabularies work well, even if they're not mathematically optimal.
questions.example: Training BPE separately on an English corpus and a code corpus to the same vocab size produces noticeably different merge rules -- the code-trained tokenizer merges common syntax patterns into single tokens that the English-trained tokenizer never learns, and vice versa for common English subwords.
commonMistakes: Assuming BPE finds the globally optimal vocabulary for a given size
Not explaining why the search for a truly optimal vocabulary is intractable at scale
Treating odd-looking token boundaries as a deliberate design choice rather than a greedy-merge artifact
Missing that the resulting vocabulary is entirely corpus-dependent
Assuming a provably optimal vocabulary would even be meaningfully better in practice given the cost tradeoff

BPE uses a greedy heuristic: merge the most frequent adjacent pair, repeat
Each merge is locally optimal but the full sequence is not guaranteed globally optimal
The resulting vocabulary is corpus-dependent and path-dependent on merge order
This is an accepted tradeoff because the greedy approach is cheap and works well in practice

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains why an optimal vocabulary search is intractable
Correctly describes the greedy merge mechanism
Explains the local-optimal-vs-global-optimal distinction
Describes the practical consequence (corpus-dependence, odd token boundaries)

questions.title: Implementing REINFORCE with a Baseline
questions.prompt: Write the policy gradient update for REINFORCE with a value baseline, and explain why the baseline is subtracted rather than simply using the raw return.
questions.code:
# log_probs: list of log pi(a_t|s_t) for the episode
# returns: list of discounted returns G_t for the episode
# baseline: a value estimate V(s_t), e.g. from a learned value function or running average

questions.modelAnswer:
The REINFORCE-with-baseline loss for a single episode is the negative sum over timesteps of log_prob(a_t | s_t) multiplied by (G_t - b(s_t)), where G_t is the discounted return from time t onward and b(s_t) is the baseline (commonly a learned state-value estimate, though a simple running average of past returns also works). The gradient of this loss is an unbiased estimator of the policy gradient as long as the baseline does not depend on the action taken, only on the state -- subtracting any state-dependent (action-independent) baseline leaves the expected gradient unchanged while reducing its variance, which is the entire point of including it.

Using the raw return G_t without a baseline works in expectation but has very high variance, especially when returns are large and noisy, because the policy gradient update then scales every action's log-probability update by the full magnitude of the return, including the large, mostly-shared part of the return that reflects how good the state itself was rather than how good that specific action was. Subtracting a baseline that estimates the expected return from that state converts G_t - b(s_t) into an estimate of the advantage -- how much better or worse this specific action's outcome was relative to what was expected from that state anyway -- which is a much lower-variance, more informative signal for the gradient to act on, without introducing bias as long as the baseline doesn't depend on the action.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The loss is just negative log_prob(a_t|s_t) times (G_t minus the baseline at that state), summed over the episode. The key property that makes this valid is that the baseline only depends on the state, not the action taken -- as long as that holds, subtracting it doesn't change the expected gradient at all, it's mathematically unbiased, it just changes the variance.

And that variance reduction is the whole reason to bother with a baseline. If you just use the raw return, you're scaling every action's gradient update by the full return, which includes a big chunk that's really about how good the state itself was, not how good that particular action was. Subtracting a baseline that estimates the expected return from that state turns G_t minus baseline into something closer to an advantage -- how much better or worse this action did relative to what you'd expect from that state anyway -- and that's a much cleaner, lower-variance signal for the gradient to learn from. In practice I'd use a learned value function as the baseline rather than a running average, since it adapts per-state rather than giving every state in the episode the same single number.

Using a single global average instead of a per-state baseline, losing most of the variance-reduction benefit

questions.title: When Quality Filtering Removes Too Much Good Data
questions.prompt: After tightening a quality-filtering classifier for a pretraining data pipeline, the model trained on the filtered data performs worse on several benchmarks than the model trained on the less-filtered previous version. How would you investigate whether the filter is the cause, and what would you look for?
questions.modelAnswer:
The first step is to directly inspect a sample of documents the tightened filter removed that the previous, looser filter kept, rather than assuming the filter is working correctly just because it is removing more content. Overly aggressive quality filters -- especially ones trained as classifiers on a narrow notion of 'high quality' text -- often disproportionately strip out content that is genuinely useful but doesn't match the classifier's narrow training signal: non-English text, code-adjacent or technical writing, dialectal or informal English, or specific domains underrepresented in whatever reference 'high quality' corpus trained the filter. Checking the removed documents' source distribution (which domains/languages lost the most content between filter versions) against which benchmarks regressed is a direct way to connect the filtering change to the specific capability loss.

A useful controlled experiment, if compute allows, is training two smaller-scale models -- one on a sample from each filter version -- and comparing benchmark performance at that smaller scale, which isolates the filter's effect from other changes that might have happened between the two full training runs. If the regression reproduces at small scale, that strongly implicates the filter rather than some other pipeline change; if it doesn't reproduce, the actual cause may lie elsewhere (a different change made alongside the filter update, or a benchmark sensitivity issue). The fix, once implicated, typically isn't abandoning filtering altogether but either loosening the filter's threshold specifically for the content types found to be disproportionately affected, or training a better-calibrated filter using training data that represents the content types that were wrongly flagged as low-quality.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I wouldn't assume the tighter filter is correct just because it's filtering out more -- I'd go pull a sample of documents it removed that the old filter kept, and actually read through them. Quality filters trained as classifiers on a narrow notion of 'good' text tend to disproportionately strip out stuff that's genuinely useful but just doesn't look like the classifier's reference data -- non-English content, technical or code-adjacent writing, informal or dialectal English, that kind of thing.

I'd check which domains or languages lost the most content between the two filter versions, and compare that against which specific benchmarks regressed -- if the filter is stripping out a lot of, say, technical writing, and the benchmarks that dropped are reasoning-heavy, that's a pretty direct link.

If I have the compute, I'd want to run a controlled small-scale test -- train two smaller models, one on a sample from each filter version, and see if the regression actually reproduces at small scale. That isolates the filter as the cause from anything else that might have changed between the two full runs. If it reproduces, I'm confident the filter is the culprit; if it doesn't, something else changed and I need to look elsewhere.

Once I've confirmed it's the filter, I usually wouldn't just loosen it back to the old threshold everywhere -- I'd try to loosen it specifically for the content types it's wrongly flagging, or retrain the filter with better-representative examples of what it was incorrectly calling low-quality.
questions.example: A real pattern: a quality classifier trained mostly on formal prose disproportionately removes Stack-Overflow-style technical Q&A text (informal tone, code snippets, short sentences); the benchmark that regressed most happens to be a coding/reasoning benchmark -- directly implicating the filter's domain blind spot.

Not directly inspecting a sample of newly-removed documents
Skipping a controlled small-scale comparison to isolate the filter's effect from other changes
Not connecting which content types were removed to which specific benchmarks regressed
Reverting the filter entirely instead of correcting its specific blind spot
keyPoints: Directly inspect removed documents rather than assuming the filter is correctly calibrated
Quality classifiers often disproportionately remove content types unlike their own reference data
Connect removed content domains/languages to which specific benchmarks regressed
A controlled small-scale comparison isolates the filter's effect from other pipeline changes
The fix is usually a targeted correction to the filter, not reverting it wholesale

Connects removed content types to specific benchmark regressions
Proposes a controlled small-scale comparison to isolate causation
Proposes a targeted fix rather than wholesale reversion

questions.title: Architecting an Evaluation Harness for a Fine-Tuned Model
questions.prompt: You need to design an evaluation harness for a model your team fine-tunes regularly, combining held-out loss, standard benchmarks, and LLM-as-judge scoring. Describe the architecture: what each component measures, how they relate, and how the harness should be structured so it stays trustworthy as the model changes.
questions.modelAnswer:
The three components measure genuinely different things and should be kept conceptually and architecturally separate rather than collapsed into one aggregate score. Held-out loss/perplexity is a cheap, fast, fully automated signal that measures how well the model predicts held-out data from a distribution similar to training, useful as an early, sensitive detector of basic training problems (a model that got measurably worse at next-token prediction on held-out data has regressed in a way that usually shows up before task-level benchmarks fully reflect it), but it doesn't directly measure task performance or instruction-following quality. Standard task benchmarks measure specific, checkable capabilities with objective scoring (accuracy on a QA set, pass rate on code execution tests), giving a hard, reproducible signal that is comparable across model versions and over time, but they can be narrow, susceptible to contamination, and slow to reflect subjective qualities like tone or helpfulness. LLM-as-judge scoring captures those subjective, harder-to-check qualities (coherence, helpfulness, adherence to a style) that the other two can't measure directly, but it introduces judge-model bias and inconsistency as a real limitation, so it should be treated as a secondary, directional signal rather than a primary gate.

Architecturally, the harness should run all three automatically on every candidate checkpoint, store results keyed by checkpoint/commit/config so historical comparisons are always possible, and define which components are hard gates (a task benchmark regression blocks a release) versus soft signals (an LLM-judge score drop prompts review but doesn't automatically block). To stay trustworthy as the model changes, the harness needs its own test set of known-good and known-bad model outputs run periodically to catch judge-model drift or benchmark contamination creeping in over time, and the benchmark set itself needs periodic refreshing with newer, uncontaminated tasks since any fixed benchmark risks slowly leaking into training data as the team iterates.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd keep these three pieces conceptually separate rather than trying to merge them into one number, because they're measuring genuinely different things. Held-out loss is cheap and fully automated -- it's a fast, sensitive early warning for basic training problems, but it doesn't tell you anything directly about task performance or whether the model is actually helpful. Standard benchmarks give you a hard, objective, comparable-over-time signal on specific capabilities, but they're narrow, can get contaminated, and don't capture subjective qualities like tone. LLM-as-judge is the only one of the three that can score those subjective qualities at all, but it comes with real judge bias and inconsistency, so I treat it as a secondary signal, not something that blocks a release on its own.

Architecturally, I'd run all three automatically on every candidate checkpoint and store the results keyed to the checkpoint, commit, and config, so I can always go back and compare historically. I'd make the hard benchmarks an actual gate -- a real regression blocks shipping -- while an LLM-judge score drop triggers a human review rather than an automatic block, since I don't fully trust the judge model's consistency on its own.

To keep this trustworthy over time, I'd build in a small fixed test set of known-good and known-bad outputs that I periodically rerun through the judge model specifically to catch judge drift, and I'd periodically refresh the benchmark set itself with newer tasks, because any fixed benchmark that sticks around long enough risks slowly leaking into training data as the team iterates on it.
questions.example: Gate structure example: held-out loss regression > 2% triggers an alert; any hard benchmark regression > 1pt blocks the release automatically; LLM-judge score drop > 5% triggers a mandatory human spot-check before shipping, but doesn't auto-block.
commonMistakes: Collapsing held-out loss, benchmarks, and LLM-judge scores into a single aggregate number
Treating LLM-as-judge as a primary release gate rather than a secondary signal
Not storing historical results keyed to checkpoint/config for trend comparison
Never refreshing the benchmark set, risking slow contamination over time
Not periodically checking the judge model itself for drift on a fixed known-good/known-bad set
keyPoints: The three components measure different things and should stay architecturally separate
Held-out loss is cheap and sensitive but not a direct task-performance measure
Standard benchmarks are objective and comparable but narrow and contamination-prone
LLM-as-judge captures subjective quality but should be a secondary signal, not a primary gate
The harness needs historical result storage, defined hard/soft gates, and periodic refresh to stay trustworthy

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what each of the three components measures
Proposes a sensible hard-gate vs soft-signal structure
Proposes historical result storage for trend comparison
Addresses long-term trustworthiness (judge drift, benchmark refresh)

questions.title: Receiving Critical Code Review on Your Own Research Code
questions.prompt: A reviewer leaves several pointed comments on your experiment PR, including one saying your evaluation script has a bug that likely inflated your reported numbers. You're fairly confident your numbers are right. How do you respond?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer resists the instinct to defend the number before actually checking the claim, since a reviewer flagging a specific, checkable bug deserves a specific, checkable response rather than a confidence-based rebuttal. The candidate should describe going to verify the claim directly -- rereading the exact line of code the reviewer pointed at, tracing through what it does with a concrete example, and if needed adding a quick print statement or unit test to see the actual behavior rather than reasoning about it abstractly -- before responding either way.

If the reviewer turns out to be right, the answer should describe acknowledging it plainly and thanking them for catching it, then actually rerunning the affected numbers rather than letting a confirmed bug sit unaddressed because the original result already got shared somewhere. If the reviewer turns out to be mistaken, the answer should describe explaining the specific reasoning or evidence that shows the code is correct (ideally with a minimal reproducible example demonstrating the behavior), rather than simply asserting confidence back at them, since the goal of the exchange is to establish the actual truth, not to win the disagreement.

The answer should also reflect that being confident in your own numbers is not evidence on its own -- confidence should update based on what checking the specific claim reveals, and a good collaborator treats a pointed, specific bug report as a gift (it's far better to be caught here than after the number ships in a report) rather than something to feel defensive about.
questions.professionalAnswer:
My first move is to actually go check, not to defend the number based on how confident I feel. I'd reread the exact line they flagged, trace through what it actually does on a concrete example, and if it's still not obvious, add a quick print or a tiny test to see the real behavior instead of reasoning about it in my head.

If it turns out they're right, I'd just say so plainly -- 'good catch, you're right, let me fix this and rerun' -- and actually go rerun the affected numbers rather than letting a confirmed bug sit there because the original number already got shared with someone. There's no upside to being slow or defensive about a real bug.

If I check and I think they're actually wrong, I wouldn't just reassert my confidence back at them -- I'd show my work. I'd put together a minimal example that demonstrates the code doing what I think it does, and walk them through it, because the point of the back-and-forth is figuring out what's actually true, not winning the exchange. And honestly, I try to treat a pointed bug report like this as a good thing, not something to get defensive about -- it's a much better outcome to catch this now in review than after the number's already in a report someone's making decisions off of.
questions.example: A productive response: 'Checked this -- you're right, the eval loop was reusing the same batch due to a seed reset bug. Reran with the fix: new number is 71.2% vs the reported 76.4%. Updating the PR now, thanks for catching it.'
commonMistakes: Defending the reported number based on confidence without actually checking the specific claim
Getting defensive or treating the review comment as a personal criticism
Checking the claim but not actually rerunning the numbers once a bug is confirmed
Dismissing the reviewer without providing a concrete counter-example if you believe they're wrong
Letting a confirmed bug sit unaddressed because the original result was already shared elsewhere
keyPoints: Verifies the specific claim directly before responding, rather than defending from confidence alone
Acknowledges plainly and reruns affected numbers if the reviewer is correct
Provides concrete evidence (not just reassertion) if the reviewer turns out to be mistaken
Treats confidence in one's own work as something to update, not evidence in itself
Treats a specific, pointed bug report as valuable rather than something to be defensive about

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Verifies the specific claim rather than defending from confidence alone
Handles being correctly corrected gracefully and reruns results
Handles the reviewer being wrong with concrete evidence, not just reassertion
Demonstrates a non-defensive, evidence-first attitude overall

questions.title: Explaining the Chinchilla Params-vs-Tokens Tradeoff to a Planning Team
questions.prompt: A planning team wants to know, at a conceptual level, why a model trained with more parameters isn't automatically better than a smaller model trained on more data, for the same total compute budget. Explain the core idea in terms they can use to reason about future training decisions.
questions.modelAnswer:
For a fixed compute budget, the total amount of compute spent during pretraining is roughly proportional to parameter count multiplied by the number of training tokens, so there is a direct tradeoff: a fixed budget split toward more parameters leaves fewer tokens to train on, and vice versa. The Chinchilla-era finding was that many large models at the time were allocating too much of their fixed budget toward parameters and not enough toward training tokens, meaning they were under-trained relative to their size -- a smaller model trained on substantially more tokens at the same total compute would have reached lower loss than the larger, under-trained model.

The conceptual takeaway for planning purposes is that parameter count by itself is not a reliable proxy for 'how good will this model be' -- what matters is whether the parameter count is matched to enough training data for the model to actually use that capacity well, and for any fixed compute budget there is a particular balance between the two that minimizes loss. This means a planning team evaluating 'should we build a bigger model' should also ask 'do we have the compute budget to train it on enough data to not under-train it,' since a bigger model trained on an unchanged token budget may actually underperform a smaller model that was properly matched to the available compute.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd frame it simply: for a fixed amount of compute, you're roughly trading parameters against training tokens -- total compute spent is close to parameters times tokens, so spending more of your budget on a bigger model means fewer tokens to train it on. The finding from the Chinchilla-era work was that a lot of big models at the time had this balance wrong -- they were big but under-trained relative to their size, and a smaller model trained on a lot more data at the same total compute would have actually done better.

For planning purposes, the thing I'd want the team to take away is that parameter count alone isn't a good proxy for 'this model will be better.' What matters is whether the parameter count is actually matched to enough data for the model to use that extra capacity. So if we're deciding whether to build a bigger model, the real question isn't just 'can we afford to train something this size,' it's 'can we afford to train something this size on enough tokens that it isn't under-trained' -- because if the token budget doesn't scale with the parameter count, we might end up with a bigger model that's actually worse than a properly-matched smaller one for the same total cost.
questions.example: Two models trained at the same total FLOP budget: Model A (large, fewer tokens) reaches a higher final loss than Model B (smaller, many more tokens), because Model A was under-trained relative to its parameter count -- a classic Chinchilla-style finding.
commonMistakes: Treating parameter count alone as a reliable proxy for model quality
Not explaining the rough proportionality between compute, parameters, and tokens
Missing that the finding was specifically about many large models being under-trained, not that small models are always better
Failing to connect the concept to an actionable planning question (is the token budget matched to the parameter count)
Treating this as a fixed universal ratio rather than something that depends on the specific compute budget
keyPoints: Compute is roughly proportional to parameters times training tokens for a fixed budget
Many large models were historically under-trained relative to their parameter count
A properly token-matched smaller model can outperform an under-trained larger one at equal compute
Parameter count alone is not a reliable proxy for model quality
Planning decisions should ask whether the token budget is matched to any proposed parameter count

Correctly explains the under-training finding

questions.prompt: Write the forward pass of a single decoder-only transformer block (causal self-attention, residual connections, layer norm, feed-forward sublayer), using pre-norm placement. Explain why pre-norm is generally preferred over post-norm for training stability.

        self.ff = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(d_model, d_ff), nn.GELU(), nn.Linear(d_ff, d_model))
        self.ln1 = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)
        self.ln2 = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)

questions.modelAnswer:
A pre-norm block applies layer normalization before each sublayer (attention or feed-forward) rather than after, with the sublayer's output added back to the pre-normalization input via a residual connection: x = x + attn(ln1(x)) followed by x = x + ff(ln2(x)). This means the residual path -- the raw addition chain running through the whole network -- never itself passes through a normalization layer; only the input to each sublayer's computation gets normalized, while the skip connection carries the unnormalized running sum straight through.

This matters for training stability because in a post-norm design (normalize after the residual addition: x = ln(x + attn(x))), the residual stream's scale gets reset by the normalization at every layer, which can make gradients flowing backward through many stacked layers unstable -- deep post-norm transformers are notoriously harder to train without careful warmup and often require a smaller learning rate to avoid divergence. Pre-norm keeps the residual stream's scale more consistent across depth since normalization only touches the branch going into each sublayer, not the main accumulating path, which empirically makes very deep transformer stacks substantially easier to train stably, at a modest cost in final model quality that is usually considered well worth the stability gain for large-scale training.
questions.professionalAnswer:
Pre-norm means I normalize before each sublayer, not after, and the sublayer's output gets added back via a residual connection to the pre-normalization input: x = x + attn(ln1(x)), then x = x + ff(ln2(x)). The key thing is that the main residual path -- the running sum of additions through the whole network -- never itself gets normalized; only the branch feeding into attention or the feed-forward layer does.

The reason that matters for stability is what happens in the alternative, post-norm, where you normalize after the residual addition. There, the residual stream's scale gets reset by normalization at every single layer, and that makes gradients flowing back through a lot of stacked layers much less stable -- deep post-norm transformers are genuinely harder to train without careful warmup and often need a smaller learning rate just to avoid diverging. Pre-norm keeps that main residual path's scale more consistent as you go deeper, since normalization only ever touches the side-branch going into a sublayer, not the accumulating path itself. That's really the whole reason pre-norm became the default for deep transformer stacks -- it trades a small amount of final quality for a training process that's much easier to get stable at scale.

def forward(self, x, causal_mask):
    x = x + self.attn(self.ln1(x), self.ln1(x), self.ln1(x), attn_mask=causal_mask, need_weights=False)[0]
    x = x + self.ff(self.ln2(x))
    return x
