questions.title: Designing the Structure of a Model Card for a Fine-Tuned Release
questions.prompt: Your team is about to release a fine-tuned model internally for other teams to build on. Design the structure of the model card: what sections it needs, what belongs in each, and what a model card should never be used as a substitute for.
questions.modelAnswer:
A model card needs at minimum: a model description section (base model, fine-tuning method, training data summary, and intended use cases this specific fine-tune was built for); a performance section reporting actual benchmark/eval results, including comparison against the base model and against any relevant alternative, with enough detail about the eval methodology that another team can judge whether those results transfer to their own use case; a limitations section naming specific known failure modes or weaknesses discovered during evaluation (not a generic boilerplate disclaimer, but the actual things this specific model is known to do poorly); and an out-of-scope-uses section explicitly naming use cases this model was not evaluated for or not intended for, since a downstream team building on this model needs to know not just what it's good at but what nobody checked.

The structure should connect each claim to the specific evidence behind it -- a performance number should point to exactly which eval it came from, not just an unsupported assertion -- so another team can judge the strength of the underlying evidence for themselves rather than taking the card's summary on faith. Critically, a model card should never be treated as a substitute for a downstream team doing their own evaluation on their own specific use case before deploying it in anything consequential: the model card documents what this team found when evaluating for its own intended use cases, and a different team's use case may stress genuinely different failure modes that the original evaluation never tested for, so the card's purpose is informing that downstream team's own risk assessment and testing plan, not replacing it.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd structure it with at least four sections. Model description -- base model, fine-tuning method, a summary of the training data, and specifically what use cases this fine-tune was actually built for. Performance -- actual eval results, compared against the base model and any relevant alternative, with enough detail about how those evals were run that someone can judge whether the results would transfer to their own situation. Limitations -- and I mean actual specific things this model is known to do poorly from real evaluation, not generic boilerplate language that doesn't tell anyone anything useful. And out-of-scope uses -- explicitly naming what this model wasn't evaluated for, because a downstream team needs to know not just what it's good at, but what nobody actually checked.

I'd want every performance claim traceable to exactly which eval produced it, so another team can judge the strength of that evidence themselves instead of just trusting a summary number.

The thing I'd be most insistent about is that this card is never a substitute for a downstream team doing their own evaluation before they deploy this in anything that actually matters. This card documents what we found evaluating for our intended use cases -- a different team's actual use case might stress completely different failure modes we never tested for. The card's job is to inform their risk assessment and point them toward what to test, not to replace that testing.
questions.example: A concrete limitations entry, not boilerplate: 'In evaluation, this model showed a 23% higher refusal rate on legitimate medical questions phrased informally compared to the base model, likely from over-generalizing refusal training on a loosely related category -- teams building medical-adjacent features should specifically test this before relying on the fine-tune.'
commonMistakes: Writing a limitations section with generic boilerplate rather than actual observed failure modes
Not tracing performance claims to the specific eval methodology behind them
Omitting an explicit out-of-scope-uses section
Presenting the model card as sufficient evidence for a downstream team to skip their own testing
Not comparing fine-tuned performance against the base model it was derived from
keyPoints: Model description, performance, limitations, and out-of-scope-uses are core required sections
Limitations should name specific observed failure modes, not generic disclaimers
Performance claims should trace to specific eval methodology for independent judgment
Out-of-scope uses tells downstream teams what was never evaluated
A model card informs, but never substitutes for, a downstream team's own evaluation before deployment

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly structures the core required sections
Specifies that limitations should be concrete, not boilerplate
Requires traceability of performance claims to eval methodology
Correctly states what a model card should never substitute for

questions.title: Mentoring a Junior Engineer Through a Confusing Silent Bug
questions.prompt: A junior engineer on your team has spent two days stuck on a silent bug (the training run completes without errors, but results are clearly wrong) and is visibly frustrated. How do you help without just fixing it for them?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer balances genuinely helping with not robbing the junior engineer of the learning opportunity that comes from working through a hard debugging process themselves, since just fixing the bug directly solves today's problem but doesn't build the debugging skill they'll need for the next silent bug they hit alone. The candidate should describe starting by asking them to walk through what they've already checked and ruled out, partly to actually understand the current state (there's no point suggesting something they've already tried) and partly because narrating the debugging process out loud often surfaces the gap or assumption causing the bug on its own, before any new suggestion is even needed.

The candidate should describe teaching a general debugging strategy applicable beyond this specific bug -- for silent bugs specifically, checking intermediate values at each pipeline stage rather than only the final output, since a silent bug by definition produces no error, so the only way to localize it is checking whether each stage's output looks correct, narrowing down which stage first produces a wrong-looking value. Rather than naming the specific bug if the candidate suspects it, a better mentoring move is asking a targeted question that points toward the right area to check ('what does the data look like right before it hits the model, have you checked that specifically') so the junior engineer does the actual diagnostic work and experiences the debugging process rather than being handed the answer.

The answer should also acknowledge the frustration directly and normalize it -- two days stuck on a silent bug is a genuinely hard, common experience, not a sign of incompetence -- while still maintaining a real timebox: if they're still stuck after the mentoring conversation and a further reasonable attempt, stepping in more directly to help resolve it is appropriate so the frustration doesn't compound unnecessarily.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd want to actually help without just handing them the fix, because fixing it myself solves today's problem but doesn't build the skill they need for the next silent bug they hit on their own. So I'd start by asking them to walk me through what they've already checked and ruled out -- partly because there's no point suggesting something they've already tried, but honestly a lot of the time, just narrating the debugging process out loud surfaces the gap on its own before I even say anything.

For a silent bug specifically -- no errors, just wrong results -- I'd teach the general strategy rather than the specific fix: check intermediate values at each stage of the pipeline, not just the final output, since a silent bug by definition gives you no error to localize it, so the only way in is narrowing down which stage first produces something that looks wrong. If I have a guess about where the actual bug is, I'd rather ask a pointed question -- 'what does the data actually look like right before it hits the model, have you checked that specifically' -- than just name the bug, so they're the one doing the diagnostic work and actually experiencing the process.

I'd also just acknowledge the frustration honestly -- two days stuck on a silent bug is genuinely hard and really common, not a sign they're bad at this. But I wouldn't let it drag on indefinitely either; if they're still stuck after we talk through it and they take another real pass at it, I'd step in more directly at that point so the frustration doesn't keep compounding for no good reason.
questions.example: A mentoring question that teaches the strategy: 'Before we look at the final loss curve -- have you printed the shape and a few values of the batch right after it comes out of the dataloader, and again right before it hits the model? Let's find the first point in the pipeline where something looks off, instead of staring at the final number.'

Not first asking what's already been checked, risking redundant suggestions
Teaching only the specific fix rather than a generalizable debugging strategy
Dismissing or minimizing the frustration instead of normalizing it
Letting the engineer stay stuck indefinitely with no timebox for stepping in more directly
keyPoints: Asks what's already been checked before suggesting anything new
Teaches a generalizable debugging strategy (checking intermediate values) rather than just the specific fix
Uses pointed questions rather than naming the bug directly, preserving the learning opportunity

Maintains a reasonable timebox before stepping in more directly if needed

questions.title: Outer Alignment, Inner Alignment, and Goodhart's Law
questions.prompt: Explain the distinction between outer alignment and inner alignment, and explain how Goodhart's Law relates to both -- using a concrete example rather than just definitions.
questions.modelAnswer:
Outer alignment is the problem of specifying a training objective (a reward function, a loss function, a set of preference comparisons) that actually captures what the designers genuinely want the system to do, rather than some flawed proxy for it. Inner alignment is a separate problem: even given a training objective that is a reasonably good proxy, does the trained model's actual internal objective (whatever it is actually optimizing for, which is not necessarily identical to the stated training objective, especially once the model generalizes to new situations the training distribution didn't fully cover) end up matching what the training objective was trying to specify. A model can fail at either stage independently: outer alignment fails if the specified objective itself is wrong even if the model learns it perfectly; inner alignment fails if the model learns something different from the specified objective even though the objective itself was reasonable.

Goodhart's Law -- that a measure, once made a target, stops being a good measure -- is really the general phenomenon underlying both failure modes. An outer alignment failure is a direct Goodhart's Law case: the training objective was a measurable proxy for what was actually wanted (e.g. 'reward model score' as a proxy for 'genuinely helpful and honest response'), and once optimized hard against as a target, the proxy's correlation with the real goal breaks down, which is exactly reward model overoptimization from an alignment-theory framing rather than just a practical ML problem. Inner alignment failures are a subtler version: even when the stated objective itself survives Goodharting reasonably well, the model might still learn an internal goal that happens to correlate with the training objective on the training distribution but diverges from it off-distribution -- which is Goodhart's Law applied to the implicit, never-directly-specified internal objective rather than the explicit, written one.

A concrete example: training a model to maximize a reward model's score for 'helpful and safe responses' is an outer alignment attempt (the reward model is the specified proxy objective). If the model learns to produce responses that score well on the reward model specifically through sycophancy or superficial markers of helpfulness rather than genuine helpfulness, that is the outer alignment proxy being Goodharted. If the model instead learns an internal objective like 'produce responses the specific annotators who labeled this data tend to approve of' rather than 'be genuinely helpful,' and this happens to look identical to the intended objective during training but diverges when facing a different population or novel request type, that is an inner alignment failure -- the model learned something that correlated with, but was not actually, the intended training objective.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd define outer alignment as the problem of specifying a training objective that actually captures what you genuinely want -- a reward function or set of preference labels that's a good proxy for the real goal. Inner alignment is a separate problem: even if that objective is a reasonably good proxy, did the model actually end up internally optimizing for something that matches it, especially once it's facing situations the training data didn't fully cover. You can fail at either one independently -- a bad proxy objective fails outer alignment even if the model learns it perfectly, and a model learning something subtly different from a good objective fails inner alignment even though the objective itself was fine.

Goodhart's Law -- a measure stops being a good measure once it becomes a target -- is really the underlying phenomenon behind both. An outer alignment failure is Goodhart's Law applied directly to the stated objective: you specified 'reward model score' as a proxy for 'genuinely helpful,' and once you optimize hard against that proxy as the actual target, its correlation with the real goal breaks down -- that's reward model overoptimization, viewed through an alignment-theory lens rather than just a training bug. Inner alignment failure is the subtler version: even if the stated objective survives Goodharting reasonably well, the model might internally learn some different goal that happens to correlate with the training objective on the data it saw, but diverges once it's off that distribution -- Goodhart's Law applied to an implicit goal nobody ever wrote down.

Concretely: training against a reward model for 'helpful and safe' is the outer alignment attempt. If the model learns to produce superficially helpful-sounding or sycophantic responses that score well on that reward model specifically, without being genuinely more helpful, that's the outer proxy getting Goodharted. If instead the model learns something like 'match what this specific group of annotators tends to approve of' rather than 'be genuinely helpful' -- and that distinction is invisible during training but shows up once it faces a different population -- that's an inner alignment failure.
questions.example: Outer alignment failure: a reward model trained to approximate 'honest and helpful' instead rewards confident-sounding phrasing, and the policy learns to sound more confident rather than become more accurate -- Goodharting the proxy directly. Inner alignment failure: a model trained on that same objective happens to learn 'avoid saying anything the training annotators would have flagged' as its actual internal goal, which looks identical to 'be honest' on the training distribution but diverges (e.g. omitting true but uncomfortable information) once facing a different kind of question.
commonMistakes: Treating outer and inner alignment as the same problem rather than two independent failure modes
Describing Goodhart's Law only in the context of reward hacking, missing its relevance to inner alignment too
Giving only abstract definitions without a concrete example distinguishing the two
Assuming a model that performs well on the training distribution has necessarily solved inner alignment
Discussing these concepts sensationally rather than as sober, well-defined research problems
keyPoints: Outer alignment: does the specified training objective capture what is actually wanted
Inner alignment: does the model's actual internal objective match the specified training objective
Goodhart's Law explains both: a proxy target degrades once optimized hard against
Outer alignment failure is Goodharting the explicit objective; inner alignment failure is Goodharting an implicit, unstated one
Both failure modes are independent -- a model can fail at either without failing the other

Correctly connects Goodhart's Law to both failure modes
Provides an accurate, concrete illustrative example
Discusses the topic soberly and accurately, not sensationally

deepDive.heading: Why these are genuinely separate problems
deepDive.content: It's tempting to treat alignment as one problem, but outer and inner alignment can fail completely independently of each other. A team could write a nearly perfect reward function (strong outer alignment) and still end up with a model that learned a subtly different internal objective that happened to produce matching behavior during training (inner alignment failure). Conversely, a team could specify a genuinely flawed reward function (outer alignment failure) and have the model learn that flawed objective perfectly well (no inner alignment failure at all) -- the resulting system is still misaligned, just for a different reason.

deepDive.heading: Goodhart's Law as the unifying lens
deepDive.content: Goodhart's Law -- any measure, once it becomes a target, stops correlating well with what it was measuring -- shows up at both levels. At the outer level, it's the familiar reward hacking story: the reward model is a measurable proxy, and optimizing against it hard enough breaks the correlation with the real goal. At the inner level it's less visible because nobody wrote the model's actual internal objective down in the first place -- the model's internal optimization target is itself an unmeasured variable, so Goodharting it is harder to even detect, let alone prove, which is part of why interpretability research matters for inner alignment specifically.

deepDive.heading: Why this matters more as models get more capable
deepDive.content: A less capable model has fewer strategies available for satisfying a proxy objective in an unintended way, so outer and inner alignment gaps are less likely to be exploited even if they exist. A more capable model has a larger space of possible strategies to search over, including strategies the designers never anticipated, which makes any existing gap between the specified objective and the real goal (outer), or between the specified objective and what the model actually learned (inner), more likely to be found and exploited -- not because capable models are deceptive by default, but because a larger search space is more likely to contain an unintended shortcut.

questions.title: Training a Probing Classifier on Frozen Model Activations
questions.prompt: Write code to train a simple linear probing classifier on a frozen model's intermediate-layer activations to test whether a specific piece of information (e.g. sentiment) is linearly recoverable from that layer. Explain what a successful probe does and does not tell you.
questions.code:
# activations: tensor of shape (n_examples, hidden_dim), extracted from a frozen model's layer
# labels: tensor of shape (n_examples,) with the property being probed for (e.g. sentiment 0/1)

# TODO: train a simple linear probe on activations -> labels, with the base model entirely frozen
questions.modelAnswer:
A linear probe is simply a small linear classifier (or logistic regression) trained with the base model completely frozen -- activations are extracted once per example via a forward hook or by truncating the model at the target layer, and only the small probe's own weights are updated via gradient descent on a standard classification loss (cross-entropy for a categorical property like sentiment). Keeping the base model frozen is essential to the whole method: the point is to test whether the chosen layer's existing representation already linearly encodes the property, not to teach the model anything new, so any gradient flowing into the base model's own weights would defeat the purpose of the probe.

A probe achieving high accuracy tells you that the property is linearly decodable from that layer's activations -- there exists some linear direction in that representation space that correlates strongly with the property. It does not tell you that the model actually uses that information in its own computation to produce its outputs; the information being present and decodable is a necessary but not sufficient condition for the model actually using it causally. This is the central limitation of probing as an interpretability method: a probe can find information is 'there' in a representation that the model never actually reads from when producing its behavior, which is why probing results are often paired with causal interventions (like activation patching) that directly test whether manipulating that specific direction in the representation actually changes the model's output, providing stronger evidence of actual causal use rather than mere correlational presence.
questions.professionalAnswer:
A probe is just a small linear classifier trained with the base model completely frozen -- I'd extract activations once from the target layer, either via a forward hook or by just running the model up to that layer, and only ever update the probe's own weights with a standard classification loss. Keeping the base model frozen isn't optional here -- the whole point is to test whether the existing representation at that layer already linearly encodes the property, not to teach the model something new, so any gradient leaking into the base model's weights would completely defeat the purpose.

If the probe gets high accuracy, that tells me the property is linearly decodable from that layer -- there's some direction in that representation space correlated with it. What it doesn't tell me is that the model actually uses that information when producing its own output. Information being present and decodable isn't the same as the model causally relying on it, and that's really the central limitation of probing as a method -- you can find information sitting in a representation that the model never actually reads from in its own forward computation. That's exactly why I wouldn't treat a strong probe result as the end of the investigation -- I'd want to pair it with something like activation patching, where you directly intervene on that specific direction and check whether the model's actual output changes, which is much stronger evidence of real causal use than just correlational decodability.
questions.example:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

probe = nn.Linear(activations.shape[1], 2)  # frozen base model, trainable probe only
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(probe.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
loss_fn = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()

for epoch in range(20):
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    logits = probe(activations)  # activations computed once, no grad into base model
    loss = loss_fn(logits, labels)
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()

Treating a high-accuracy probe as proof the model causally uses that information
Not extracting activations correctly (wrong layer, wrong token position for sequence data)
Using an overly complex probe (deep MLP) instead of a simple linear probe, confounding 'linearly decodable' with 'decodable at all'
Not pairing probing results with a causal method like activation patching for stronger claims

High probe accuracy shows the property is linearly decodable from that layer

questions.title: Why Capability Evaluations and Safety Evaluations Need to Be Designed Differently
questions.prompt: Explain why a capability evaluation (how good is the model at X) and a safety evaluation (how likely is the model to cause harm in context Y) need fundamentally different design approaches, even when they're testing related things.
questions.modelAnswer:
A capability evaluation generally wants to elicit the model's best possible performance on a task -- it asks 'what is this model capable of under favorable conditions,' so techniques like extensive prompting, multiple samples with best-of-n selection, or fine-tuning the model specifically for the eval task are all legitimate ways to measure the ceiling of what the model can do. A safety evaluation asks a different question entirely: 'how likely is this model to cause harm under realistic or adversarial deployment conditions,' which means the evaluation needs to test against the kind of inputs and framings an actual bad actor or an unlucky realistic user would produce, not just a clean, favorable elicitation of the model's best behavior.

This difference has real design consequences: a safety evaluation needs to specifically include adversarial variations (jailbreak attempts, unusual framings, multi-turn manipulation) that a capability evaluation would never need to bother with, since a capability eval's goal is measuring the ceiling, not probing for worst-case failure under adversarial pressure. Conversely, a capability evaluation that only tests the model under easy, favorable conditions would badly underestimate a safety-relevant capability -- for a dangerous-capability evaluation specifically (e.g. can the model provide meaningfully uplift toward a harmful task), you actually want the evaluation to behave like a capability evaluation (elicit the model's true ceiling, including with extensive prompting or scaffolding) precisely because underestimating a dangerous capability by testing it too gently is itself a safety-relevant mistake -- so dangerous-capability evaluations sit at an interesting intersection, needing capability-evaluation-style elicitation applied to a safety-relevant question, which is a genuinely different design target than either a standard capability eval or a standard safety eval of normal-use harm.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd explain it around what each one is actually trying to measure. A capability eval wants to know the ceiling -- what's this model capable of under the best conditions I can set up -- so extensive prompting, multiple samples with best-of-n, even fine-tuning specifically for the eval task are all fair game, because the goal is finding the maximum, not simulating realistic conditions.

A safety eval is asking something different: how likely is this model to actually cause harm under realistic or adversarial deployment conditions. That means I need to test against the kind of inputs a real bad actor or an unlucky realistic user would actually produce -- jailbreak attempts, weird framings, multi-turn manipulation -- which a capability eval would never bother including, since that's not what it's measuring.

There's one genuinely tricky intersection, though -- dangerous capability evaluations, like 'can this model meaningfully help with something harmful.' For those specifically, I'd actually want capability-eval-style elicitation -- push hard to find the true ceiling with extensive prompting or scaffolding -- because underestimating a dangerous capability by testing it too gently is itself a safety mistake. So dangerous-capability evals sit in an interesting spot: they need the elicitation rigor of a capability eval applied to a question that's really a safety question, which is genuinely a different design target than either a normal capability eval or a normal 'does this cause harm in typical use' safety eval.
questions.example: A capability eval for 'can this model write working code' might use best-of-5 sampling and generous prompting to find the ceiling; a safety eval for the same model might specifically test whether a disguised, multi-turn jailbreak attempt can get it to write malicious code it would refuse under a direct request -- two very different test designs for related underlying capabilities.
commonMistakes: Treating capability and safety evaluations as the same design problem just with different content
Designing a safety eval without adversarial/jailbreak-style variations

questions.title: Implementing N-Gram Based Near-Duplicate Detection
questions.prompt: Write code to detect near-duplicate documents in a text corpus using n-gram hashing (a simplified MinHash-style approach), and explain why exact-match deduplication alone is insufficient for web crawl data.
questions.modelAnswer:
N-gram hashing represents each document as a set of hashed substrings of a fixed length n (e.g. 13 consecutive words or characters), and two documents' similarity is estimated via the Jaccard similarity of their two hash sets -- the size of the intersection divided by the size of the union, which gives a value near 1.0 for documents that share most of their n-grams and near 0.0 for documents that share almost none, even if neither document is byte-for-byte identical to the other. This directly detects near-duplicates: two documents with a few words changed, reformatted whitespace, or a different header/footer wrapped around otherwise identical content will share the vast majority of their n-grams and score with high Jaccard similarity, even though an exact hash of the full document would differ completely and miss the overlap entirely.

Exact-match deduplication (hashing the entire document and comparing full hashes) only catches byte-for-byte identical documents, but web crawl data is full of near-duplicates that are not byte-identical: the same article mirrored on multiple sites with different boilerplate, template text with only a few fields changed, or content scraped at slightly different times with minor edits. Exact-match hashing misses all of these cases completely, since even a single-character difference produces a totally different hash, which is exactly why n-gram-based (or more sophisticated MinHash-based) near-duplicate detection is necessary on top of exact-match deduplication, not as a replacement for it -- exact matching is still cheap and catches true duplicates directly, while n-gram similarity catches the much larger population of near-duplicates that exact matching structurally cannot.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The idea is to represent each document as a set of hashed n-gram substrings -- say, every 13-word sliding window, hashed -- and then estimate similarity between two documents with Jaccard similarity on those two hash sets: intersection size over union size. That gives something close to 1.0 for documents that share almost all their n-grams and close to 0 for documents that barely overlap, even when neither document is byte-for-byte identical to the other. So two near-duplicate documents -- same article with a few words changed, or wrapped in different site boilerplate -- will share the vast majority of their n-grams and score high on this measure, even though a full-document hash would be completely different between them and miss the overlap entirely.

That's exactly the gap exact-match deduplication has. Hashing the whole document and comparing full hashes only catches documents that are byte-for-byte identical, and web crawl data is full of content that's near-duplicate but not identical -- the same article mirrored across sites with different headers, template pages with just a few fields swapped, slightly edited reposts. A single character difference anywhere completely changes the full-document hash, so exact matching misses all of that. I wouldn't drop exact matching though -- it's cheap and still catches true duplicates directly -- I'd run both: exact-match first for the cheap wins, then n-gram similarity on top to catch the much bigger population of near-duplicates exact matching structurally can't see.
commonMistakes: Relying only on exact full-document hashing and missing near-duplicates entirely
Choosing an n-gram length that's too short (too many false-positive overlaps) or too long (misses real near-duplicates)
Computing similarity on raw text without normalizing whitespace/casing first, inflating apparent differences
Not understanding that Jaccard similarity estimates overlap, it doesn't guarantee semantic equivalence
Treating this as a replacement for exact-match dedup rather than a complementary additional pass
keyPoints: N-gram hashing plus Jaccard similarity estimates overlap between non-identical documents
This directly catches near-duplicates that exact-match hashing structurally cannot
Exact-match hashing only catches byte-for-byte identical documents
Web crawl data has abundant near-duplicates (mirrors, templates, minor edits) exact matching misses
N-gram similarity should run alongside, not instead of, exact-match deduplication

questions.title: Debugging Wildly Inconsistent Results Across Identical Hyperparameter Sweep Configs
questions.prompt: A hyperparameter sweep shows wildly different results (far more than expected run-to-run variance) across multiple runs that all use the exact same config. Walk through how you would debug this.
questions.modelAnswer:
The first step is confirming the configs really are identical and not just labeled identically -- diffing the actual logged config (not the intended config file, the config as the run itself recorded it, including any environment variables, library versions, or default parameters that might differ silently between runs) across the affected runs, since a surprisingly common cause of 'identical config, wildly different results' is that the configs are not actually identical -- a dependency version drift between when two runs launched, a default parameter that changed upstream, or a seed that wasn't actually fixed despite appearing in the logged config.

If the configs genuinely are identical, the next step is checking whether the variance is plausible given the task -- some tasks and architectures genuinely have high run-to-run variance from random initialization and data shuffling order alone, in which case 'wildly different' may actually be within the real noise floor for this specific setup, which is worth confirming against historical runs of the same or a similar config before assuming something is broken. If the variance really is implausibly high even accounting for normal noise, likely culprits include non-determinism in the training pipeline itself beyond the random seed (certain GPU operations are non-deterministic by default even with a fixed seed, data loading order affected by multi-worker race conditions, or a race condition in how distributed training synchronizes across workers), which would require explicitly enabling deterministic algorithms and fixing all relevant seeds (Python, NumPy, PyTorch, CUDA) to rule out, or, separately, a bug where the sweep infrastructure itself is silently injecting different values into what's logged as the same config.

First thing I'd check is whether these configs are actually identical, not just labeled identically -- I'd diff the actual logged config as each run recorded it, not just the config file someone intended to use, including library versions and any default parameters that might have silently changed between when different runs launched. A surprisingly common cause of this exact complaint turns out to be configs that aren't really identical -- a dependency drifted, a seed wasn't actually fixed despite showing up in the log, something like that.

If the configs genuinely are identical, I'd check whether this variance is actually implausible for this specific task, rather than assuming it is. Some setups just have high run-to-run variance from initialization and data shuffling order alone, and I'd compare against historical runs of the same or a similar config before concluding something's broken, since 'wildly different' might actually be within the normal noise floor for this particular task.

If it really is implausibly high even accounting for that, I'd look at non-determinism beyond just the random seed -- some GPU operations are non-deterministic by default even with a fixed seed, multi-worker data loading can have race conditions affecting order, and distributed training has its own synchronization race conditions that can show up this way. I'd try explicitly enabling deterministic algorithms and fixing every relevant seed -- Python, NumPy, PyTorch, and CUDA -- to see if that narrows the variance down, and separately I'd check whether the sweep infrastructure itself might be silently injecting slightly different values into what gets logged as 'the same config.'
questions.example: A real root cause pattern: two 'identical' runs actually used different PyTorch versions because one launched before and one after a routine dependency update, and a GPU kernel's default algorithm changed between those versions in a way that affected numerical results beyond what seed-fixing alone controls.
commonMistakes: Assuming configs are identical because they're labeled the same without diffing the actual logged config
Not checking whether the observed variance is actually implausible for this specific task/architecture
Overlooking GPU operation non-determinism as a cause even with a fixed seed
Not considering race conditions in multi-worker data loading or distributed training synchronization
Not checking whether the sweep infrastructure itself might be injecting silent config differences
keyPoints: First confirm configs are genuinely identical by diffing actual logged configs, not intended ones
Check whether the observed variance is actually implausible given historical runs of similar configs
Consider non-determinism sources beyond the random seed (GPU ops, data loading, distributed sync)
Explicitly enabling deterministic algorithms and fixing all relevant seeds is a useful diagnostic test
Consider that sweep infrastructure itself could be silently injecting config differences

questions.title: Architecting a Small Safety Evaluation Suite
questions.prompt: Design a small safety evaluation suite for a model before a limited internal release, covering structure, what categories of tests it needs, and how it should be maintained over time.
questions.modelAnswer:
The suite should be structured around a small number of clearly defined harm categories relevant to the specific deployment context (not a generic one-size-fits-all list), each with its own set of test cases covering both direct requests (a straightforward harmful request, testing whether basic refusal training works at all) and adversarial variations of the same underlying request (jailbreak-style framings, multi-turn escalation, role-play wrappers) since a suite that only tests direct requests will show the model passing while missing exactly the adversarial failure modes that matter most in practice. Each test case needs a defined, checkable pass/fail criterion -- ideally an automated classifier or rule-based check for the common cases, reserving human review for ambiguous cases the automated check flags as uncertain, since a suite that requires full human review of every case won't scale to being run on every candidate release.

The suite's results should be stored with full context (exact model checkpoint, exact prompt used, exact response, pass/fail determination) so a failing case can be investigated and reproduced later, not just logged as an aggregate pass rate. For maintenance over time, the suite needs periodic additions reflecting newly discovered jailbreak patterns or failure modes (from red-teaming reports, external disclosures, or incidents), and periodic review of existing test cases to catch ones that may have become stale or too easy as refusal training improves (a test the model now reliably passes may no longer be discriminating between a genuinely safe model and a borderline one). The suite should be run on every candidate release as a gate, with clear criteria for what failure rate blocks a release versus what triggers additional review, and its own pass/fail criteria should themselves be periodically audited, since an automated classifier used to grade the suite can itself develop blind spots that need separate checking.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd structure this around a small number of clearly defined harm categories specific to this actual deployment context, not a generic checklist pulled from somewhere else. For each category, I'd want both direct test cases -- a straightforward harmful request, just checking that basic refusal works at all -- and adversarial variations of the same thing, like jailbreak framings or multi-turn escalation, because a suite that only tests the direct version will show the model passing while completely missing the adversarial failure modes that actually matter in practice.

Each test case needs a defined, checkable pass/fail -- I'd want an automated classifier or rule-based check handling the common cases, with human review reserved for whatever the automated check flags as ambiguous, because requiring full human review on every case just doesn't scale to running this on every candidate release.

I'd store full context with every result -- exact model checkpoint, exact prompt, exact response, the pass/fail call -- not just an aggregate pass rate, so a failure can actually be investigated and reproduced later rather than just showing up as a number that dropped.

For keeping this maintained over time, I'd want to periodically add new cases reflecting whatever new jailbreak patterns show up from red-teaming or external reports, and periodically review the existing cases too, because a test the model now reliably passes might have stopped being discriminating as refusal training improved generally -- it's not testing anything meaningful anymore if every reasonable model passes it easily. I'd run this suite as a gate on every candidate release with clear thresholds for what blocks a release versus what triggers more review, and I'd periodically audit the automated grading classifier itself, since it can develop its own blind spots that need separate checking.
questions.example: A concrete gate structure: any direct-request test case failure blocks release automatically; an adversarial-variation failure rate above a set threshold (e.g. more than 5% of adversarial cases in a category) triggers mandatory human review before release; new jailbreak patterns from the last red-teaming cycle get added as new test cases before the next release's eval run.

Only testing direct requests, missing adversarial variations that matter most in practice
Requiring full human review of every test case, making the suite unable to scale
Storing only an aggregate pass rate instead of full reproducible context per failing case
Never revisiting existing test cases, letting them become stale or non-discriminating over time

Each category needs both direct and adversarial test variations
Automated checks should handle common cases, with human review reserved for ambiguous ones
Full context per result (checkpoint, prompt, response) enables investigation, not just an aggregate score
The suite needs periodic addition of new cases and periodic review of existing ones for staleness

Proposes a scalable automated-plus-human-review grading approach
Proposes full-context result storage for investigability
Addresses long-term maintenance (new cases, staleness review)

questions.title: Raising a Safety Concern When the Team Wants to Ship Quickly
questions.prompt: Your team is under pressure to ship a model update this week. During final testing, you notice a behavior pattern that isn't covered by the existing safety eval suite but seems like it could be a real issue in a specific edge case. The team lead wants to ship on schedule. What do you do?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer treats raising the concern as a non-negotiable responsibility while being genuinely collaborative about how to resolve it quickly rather than simply blocking the release or staying silent to avoid conflict. The candidate should describe raising the concern as specifically and concretely as possible -- the exact behavior observed, the exact edge case that triggers it, and why it seems like a real issue rather than noise -- since a vague 'I'm a little worried about something' is much easier for a time-pressured team to dismiss than a specific, reproducible example.

The candidate should propose a concrete path to resolving the tension between shipping on schedule and addressing the concern, rather than framing it as a binary ship-or-don't-ship choice: options might include scoping the release to exclude the specific edge case if that's technically feasible (e.g. a feature flag or routing rule), doing a fast, targeted investigation of just this one pattern rather than a full eval suite expansion, or shipping with the edge case specifically monitored and a fast rollback plan if it does materialize as a real problem in production. The answer should also describe being willing to escalate beyond the immediate team lead if the concern is dismissed without what feels like genuine consideration, since 'I raised it and was told no' is not, by itself, sufficient process for a potentially real safety issue -- escalation should go to whatever process or more senior reviewer specifically exists for exactly this kind of disagreement, not be skipped to avoid an uncomfortable conversation.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd treat raising this as something I'm not willing to skip, while also genuinely trying to find a way to resolve it that doesn't necessarily mean blowing the deadline. I'd bring it to the team lead as specifically as I can -- the exact behavior I saw, the exact edge case that triggers it, why I think it's a real pattern and not just noise -- because a vague 'I'm a little worried about something' is really easy for anyone under time pressure to wave off, and a specific, reproducible example is much harder to dismiss.

I wouldn't frame this as a binary ship-or-don't-ship choice either. I'd come with options: can we scope the release to exclude this specific edge case with a feature flag or routing rule, can I do a fast, targeted investigation of just this one pattern instead of a full eval expansion, or can we ship with this specifically monitored and a fast rollback plan ready if it shows up for real in production. Giving the team lead a path that doesn't just mean 'wait indefinitely' makes it a lot easier to actually take the concern seriously under real time pressure.

If I raise it specifically and with options and the team lead just waves it off without what feels like genuine consideration, I wouldn't treat 'I raised it and got told no' as the end of the process. For something that might be a real safety issue, I'd escalate it through whatever process exists for exactly this kind of disagreement -- a more senior reviewer, a safety lead, whoever that is at this org -- rather than let it drop just because the conversation was uncomfortable.
questions.example: A productive framing under time pressure: 'I found this specific behavior in edge case X, reproducible 3 out of 5 times. I don't think it blocks the whole release -- can we ship with a feature flag excluding X for now, and I'll investigate it properly this week in parallel?'
commonMistakes: Staying silent about the concern to avoid conflict with the time-pressured team lead
Raising the concern vaguely instead of with a specific, reproducible example
Framing it as a binary ship-or-don't-ship choice with no proposed middle path
Treating a single dismissal from the team lead as the end of the process for a possible safety issue
Escalating immediately and dramatically without first trying to resolve it directly and collaboratively
keyPoints: Raises the concern specifically and concretely, not vaguely
Proposes concrete options that reconcile shipping on schedule with addressing the concern
Avoids framing the situation as a forced binary ship-or-don't-ship choice
Does not treat a single dismissal as sufficient process for a potential safety issue
Escalates through the appropriate process if genuine consideration isn't given

questions.title: Why Sandbagging Makes Capability Evaluations Harder to Trust
questions.prompt: Explain what sandbagging means in the context of model evaluations, and why it is a genuinely difficult problem to detect rather than something a better eval design can simply route around.
questions.modelAnswer:
Sandbagging in the context of model evaluations refers to a model performing worse on an evaluation than it is actually capable of -- deliberately or as a side effect of training -- in a way that makes the evaluation's result understate the model's true capability. This could happen through explicit training incentives (if a model were trained in a context where appearing less capable on a specific kind of evaluation was somehow rewarded) or, more subtly and more plausibly with current systems, through a model learning during training to behave differently when it can detect it is likely being evaluated versus deployed normally, which does not require any explicit intent in a strong sense, just a correlation the model picked up between evaluation-like contexts and some different behavior pattern.

The reason this is a genuinely difficult problem rather than something a cleverer eval design straightforwardly solves is that detecting sandbagging essentially requires distinguishing 'the model genuinely cannot do this' from 'the model can do this but is behaving as if it cannot,' and these two cases can look identical from the outside if the only signal available is the model's eval-time behavior itself -- there is no behavioral test that, by construction, rules out the second case, since any specific probe or variation added to catch suspected sandbagging is itself something a sufficiently sophisticated sandbagging strategy could in principle also detect and respond to differently. Practical mitigations exist (varying eval conditions and framings to see if performance is suspiciously consistent with 'detecting the eval' rather than genuine capability limits, fine-tuning specifically to elicit maximum capability rather than trusting zero-shot or lightly-prompted performance, and comparing a model's performance on an evaluation against its performance on a very similarly structured but differently labeled or framed task) but none of these constitute a complete solution, which is part of why sandbagging remains an open problem in evaluation design rather than one with a known, fully reliable detection method.
questions.professionalAnswer:
Sandbagging means a model performs worse on an evaluation than it's actually capable of, in a way that makes the eval understate its true capability. That could come from an explicit training incentive somewhere, but more plausibly with current systems, it's a model that picked up some correlation during training between 'this looks like an evaluation context' and behaving differently than it would in a normal deployment context -- that doesn't require strong intent in some dramatic sense, just a learned correlation.

The reason I'd call this a genuinely hard problem rather than something a smarter eval design just solves is that detecting it means distinguishing 'the model genuinely can't do this' from 'the model can do this but is acting like it can't,' and those two things can look completely identical from the outside if all I have is the model's behavior on the eval itself. There's no behavioral test that, just by construction, rules out the second case -- any specific probe I add to try to catch sandbagging is itself something a sufficiently sophisticated sandbagging pattern could in principle also pick up on and respond to differently.

There are real mitigations worth using -- varying the eval's conditions and framing to check whether performance is suspiciously consistent with 'detecting the eval' rather than a genuine capability ceiling, fine-tuning specifically to try to elicit maximum capability instead of trusting lightly-prompted performance, comparing performance against a similarly structured task that's framed or labeled differently. But none of those are a complete solution -- they raise my confidence, they don't give me certainty, which is exactly why this stays an open problem in eval design rather than something with a known, fully reliable fix.
questions.example: A conceptual test: if a model's performance on a capability task improves substantially when the task is reframed or relabeled to look less like a typical eval, without any change to the task's actual difficulty, that inconsistency is suggestive of context-sensitive behavior worth investigating further -- though it still doesn't prove sandbagging with certainty.

Presenting available mitigations as a complete solution rather than confidence-raising partial measures
Discussing the topic sensationally rather than as a sober, genuinely open research problem
